slides.title: Part 1. Molecules and Materials
text: Part 1. Molecules and Materials

slides.title: Molecules and Materials
text: Molecules and Materials
• A molecule is a group of two or more
atoms chemically bonded together,
such as a single water molecule (H₂O).
• A material, is a larger collection of
molecules that forms a macroscopic
substance with specific properties, like
water or a piece of metal.

slides.title: 1D Molecular Representations: SMILES & InChI
text: 1D Molecular Representations: SMILES & InChI
• These text-based strings encode molecular connectivity in a compact,
linear format suitable for sequence models.

slides.title: 2D Molecular Representations: Molecular Graphs
text: 2D Molecular Representations: Molecular Graphs
• This is the most natural representation of a molecule's connectivity,
where atoms are nodes and bonds are edges.
• Node features can include atomic number and charge, while edge
features can include bond type (single, double, etc.).

slides.title: 2D Molecular Representations: Fingerprints
text: 2D Molecular Representations: Fingerprints
• A fingerprint is a fixed-length vector (usually of 0s and 1s) that indicates
the presence or absence of predefined chemical substructures.
• Computationally cheap and are a standard input for classical machine learning models.

slides.title: 3D Molecular Representations: Atomic Coordinates
text: 3D Molecular Representations: Atomic Coordinates
• Using the x, y, z coordinates of each atom
provides a complete, physically realistic
description essential for geometry-
dependent problems.
• A molecule's 3D conformation is largely
determined by the low-energy rotational
barriers of its torsional (dihedral) angles.

text: Chirality: When Your Mirror Image is Different
• Chiral molecules are non-superimposable on their mirror images, a
subtle 3D property that 2D representations like graphs completely miss.

counter clock-wise order:

• D-Alanine: C[C@H](N)C(=O)O

slides.title: Molecular Symmetry
text: Molecular Symmetry
• We can describe molecules not just by coordinates but by their inherent
symmetries (rotations, reflections).
• Point groups are a classification system that neatly categorizes all possible symmetries a finite
molecule can possess.
Some crystals are “more
symmetric” than others…

slides.title: Unit Cells and Lattices
text: Unit Cells and Lattices
• Bravais lattice: distinct lattice types
(14 in 3D) describing all possible
periodic arrangements of points.
• These include primitive and centered lattices
for each crystal system
• Each lattice type is associated with a
set of translations that leaves the
crystal invariant.
• NOT associated with a particular group!

slides.title: Symmetry in Crystal Structures
text: Symmetry in Crystal Structures
• Crystals exhibit symmetry operations:
• translations, rotations, reflections, inversion that map
the crystal onto itself.
• Translational symmetry:
• the repeating lattice means a translation by one unit cell
leaves the crystal unchanged
• Point symmetry:
• Rotations or inversions about lattice points,                       Allows additional
e.g., a cube has 90° rotational axes and mirror planes.             translation
• Combination of point symmetries with translations gives
the full space group symmetry
Allows 6-fold rotation

slides.title: Space Group Symmetry
text: Space Group Symmetry
• Space groups (230 distinct groups in 3D) which enumerate all
combinations of rotations, mirrors, glide planes, screw axes with
translations that a crystal can have.
• Obtained from removing duplicates in 14x32 combinations.
2D space groups

slides.title: How Symmetry Constrains Properties
text: How Symmetry Constrains Properties
• A molecule's symmetry determines which properties it can have; for
example, a molecule with a center of inversion cannot have a permanent
dipole moment.
Some crystals are “more
symmetric” than others…

slides.title: The Importance of Defects
text: The Importance of Defects
• Real materials are never perfect,
and defects like vacancies or
impurities often control their most
useful properties.

slides.title: The Wavefunction
text: The Wavefunction
• The wavefunction is a mathematical
function that describes everything we
know about an electron in a system.
• While the function itself is abstract, its
square, 𝜓 2 , gives us something
concrete: the probability of finding an
electron at a specific point.
• For now, think of it as a mathematical
description of everything we know
about a particular quantum system.           22

slides.title: Atomic Orbitals (s, p, d, f)
text: Atomic Orbitals (s, p, d, f)
• The solutions to the hydrogen
equation give us the familiar atomic
orbitals (s, p, d, f).
• Orbital: each of the actual or
potential patterns of electron density
that may be formed in an atom or
molecule by one or more electrons.

slides.title: Approximations…
text: Approximations…
• In fact, the introduced Schrodinger equation is
a simplified version.
• We use Born-Oppenheimer approximation:
the wave functions of atomic nuclei and
electrons in a molecule can be treated
separately.
• We also ignore time-dependency.

• Wavefunctions are system-specific and not atom-specific.
• Due to the system change,

slides.title: Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals
text: Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals
• Atomic interactions can be approximated by linear combinations
• Bonding molecular orbital: The electrons in this orbital are found between the two nuclei,
effectively "gluing" the atoms together.
• Antibonding molecular orbital: The electrons in this orbital are pushed away from the space
between the nuclei.

slides.title: Density Functional Theory (DFT)
text: Density Functional Theory (DFT)
• To study real molecules, we rely on powerful approximate methods like
Density Functional Theory (DFT).
• Instead of tracking every electron's complicated wavefunction, DFT
cleverly focuses on a simpler property: the total electron density.
• DFT is a workhorse in chemistry and materials science, but it's still
computationally demanding, often 𝑂(𝑁 3 ) or even 𝑂(𝑁 6 ).

slides.title: Part 3. Electronic Properties:
text: Part 3. Electronic Properties:
From Orbitals to Bands

slides.title: How Electrons Behave in Chemical Systems
text: How Electrons Behave in Chemical Systems
• As we know from the Schrödinger equation, an electron in an atom
doesn't just circle the nucleus like a planet.
• Instead, its location is described by an atomic orbital, which is a
probability map of where the electron is likely to be.
• Each atomic orbital has a distinct energy level.

slides.title: Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO)
text: Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO)
• Molecular orbital with the highest energy
level that contains at least one electron.
• Think of all the electrons in a molecule filling up the
available energy orbitals from the lowest energy to the
highest.
• The HOMO is the very last "room" that an electron
occupies.
• This orbital is associated with a molecule's ability to
donate electrons. An electron in a high-energy state
is easier to remove and give to another molecule.

slides.title: Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital.
text: Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital.
• Molecular orbital with the lowest energy
level that is empty of electrons.
• This is the very next "room" available
for an electron to jump into.
• This orbital is associated with a molecule’s
ability to accept electrons.
• It's the most accessible place for
an incoming electron to go.

slides.title: HOMO-LUMO Gap
text: HOMO-LUMO Gap
• This gap is a critical measure of a molecule’s
excitability and chemical stability.
• A molecule with a large energy gap is generally more
stable and less reactive. It takes a lot of energy to "excite"
an electron from the HOMO to the LUMO.
• A molecule with a small energy gap is typically more
reactive and less stable. It requires less energy for an
electron to make the jump, allowing it to participate more
readily in chemical reactions.

slides.title: In Crystals: Electronic Band Structure
text: In Crystals: Electronic Band Structure
• Now, let's scale this up. Instead of two
atoms, imagine a vast number of them,
as you would find in a solid material.
• All of their atomic orbitals combine to form a
massive number of molecular orbitals.
• Because there are so many of these orbitals, their
energy levels are incredibly close together.
• They are so close that they essentially form a
continuous range of allowed energies, which we
call an energy band.

slides.title: The Electronic Band Structure of Solids
text: The Electronic Band Structure of Solids
• Band types:
• Valence Band: This is the highest energy band that is
filled with electrons. You can think of these as the
electrons that are involved in bonding.
• Conduction Band: This is the next higher energy
band, which is mostly empty. For an electron to move
freely and conduct electricity, it needs to jump into
this band.
• Band Gap: This is a crucial "forbidden zone" of
energy that separates the valence and conduction
bands. No electron can exist with an energy level
within the band gap.

slides.title: Band Gaps: Metals, Insulators, Semiconductors
text: Band Gaps: Metals, Insulators, Semiconductors
• Electrical conductivity is decided by band gap:
• Metals (Conductors): No band gap! Electrons can easily
move
into the conduction band and conduct electricity.
• Insulators: These materials have a very large band gap. It
takes a great deal of energy to excite an electron from the
valence band to the conduction band.
• Semiconductors: The band gap in semiconductors is small.
With a little energy (like from heat or light), electrons can
jump the gap and move into the conduction band.

slides.title: Part 4. Intra- and Inter-Molecular Forces
text: Part 4. Intra- and Inter-Molecular Forces

slides.title: From Quantum Mechanics to Chemical Forces
text: From Quantum Mechanics to Chemical Forces
• While the Schrödinger equation describes all energy and forces in a
system, we use simplified models and categories for practical
understanding.
• We can group forces into two main types:
• Intramolecular: Strong forces that hold
atoms together within a molecule
(e.g., covalent bonds).
• Intermolecular: Weaker forces
that cause molecules to attract
each other.

slides.title: Intramolecular Forces: Covalent Bonds
text: Intramolecular Forces: Covalent Bonds
• Covalent bonds, formed by sharing
electrons, are the strong, directional links
that define a molecule's structure.
• This type of bond typically forms between
nonmetal atoms that have similar
tendencies to attract electrons.

slides.title: Intramolecular Forces: Ionic & Metallic Bonds
text: Intramolecular Forces: Ionic & Metallic Bonds
• Ionic bonds result from electrostatic attraction between charged ions.
• Found in: Compounds formed between metals and nonmetals, such as sodium chloride (NaCl)
and magnesium oxide (MgO)
• Found in: Metallic elements and alloys, such as iron, copper, gold, and brass.

slides.title: Intramolecular Forces: Ionic & Metallic Bonds
text: Intramolecular Forces: Ionic & Metallic Bonds
• Metallic bonds involve a "sea" of delocalized electrons.
• Found in: Metallic elements and alloys, such as iron, copper, gold, and brass.

slides.title: Intermolecular Forces: Hydrogen Bonds
text: Intermolecular Forces: Hydrogen Bonds
• A hydrogen (H) atom, covalently bonded to a more electronegative donor
atom or group (Dn), interacts with another electronegative atom bearing a
lone pair of electrons—the hydrogen bond acceptor (Ac).
• This stronger, highly directional interaction is critical in biological systems like DNA and proteins.

slides.title: Intermolecular Forces: Dipole-Dipole Force
text: Intermolecular Forces: Dipole-Dipole Force
• Attractive forces that occur between
polar molecules with permanent partial
positive and negative charges.
• An electric dipole deals with the
separation of the positive and negative
electric charges found in any
electromagnetic system.

slides.title: Intermolecular Forces: London Dispersion Forces
text: Intermolecular Forces: London Dispersion Forces
• These short-range attractions arise from
temporary, fluctuating dipoles and are
present in all molecules.
• The term "Van der Waals forces" is
sometimes used to collectively refer to both
London dispersion and dipole-dipole
forces.

slides.title: A Hierarchy of Forces
text: A Hierarchy of Forces
• Intramolecular Forces (Strong - Holding molecules together):
• Covalent Bonds: ~200–800 kJ/mol
• Ionic Bonds: ~100–400 kJ/mol
• Intermolecular Forces (Weak - Pulling molecules together):
• Hydrogen Bonds: ~10–40 kJ/mol (a special, strong type of dipole-dipole force)
• Dipole-Dipole Forces: ~5–20 kJ/mol
• London Dispersion Forces: ~0.1–10 kJ/mol

text: Part 5. Statistical Mechanics:
From One Molecule to Many

slides.title: The Ensemble View of Matter
text: The Ensemble View of Matter
• Instead of one perfect structure, a real system is an "ensemble" of
countless molecules constantly moving and exploring different energy
states.

slides.title: The Boltzmann Distribution
text: The Boltzmann Distribution
• The Boltzmann distribution gives the probability for a system with state 𝑞:
𝑃 𝑞 ∝ 𝑒 −𝐸(𝑞)/𝑘𝐵 𝑇
• It tells us that high-energy states are exponentially
less likely than low-energy states.
• As temperature increases, higher energy
states become more accessible.

slides.title: Gibbs Free Energy
text: Gibbs Free Energy
• Ultimate decider of spontaneity for chemical & biological processes:
𝐺 = −𝑘𝐵 𝑇 ln 𝑍 = ln ∫ 𝑒 −𝐸(𝑞)/𝑘𝐵 𝑇 𝑑𝑞
• Maximum amount of non-volume expansion “work”
that can be extracted from a closed system.
• A system at constant temperature and pressure will
spontaneously evolve to minimize its Gibbs Free Energy.
• Gibbs free energy 𝐺 = 𝐻 − 𝑇𝑆 is can also be expressed
using entropy 𝐻 and enthalpy 𝑆.

slides.title: Entropy and Enthalpy
text: Entropy and Enthalpy
• Recall definition of Gibbs free energy: 𝐺 = 𝐻 − 𝑇𝑆.
• Enthalpy is averaged internal energy:
𝐻 = ∫ 𝑝 𝑞 𝐸 𝑞 𝑑𝑞
• Entropy is energy “locked up” by system disorder:
𝑆 = ∫ 𝑝 𝑞 log 𝑝 𝑞 𝑑𝑞
• Second law of thermodynamics: For a process to happen, a certain amount of the
system's energy must be invested to reduce/increase disorder.

slides.title: Chemistry is About Change
text: Chemistry is About Change
• We now move from static structures to the dynamic processes of
chemical reactions and conformational changes.
• Conformational changes: Molecules can change their shape without
breaking bonds (e.g., rotation around a single bond).
• Chemical reactions: Old bonds break and new bonds form,
leading to entirely new molecules.

slides.title: Potential Energy Surface (PES)
text: Potential Energy Surface (PES)
• PES is a high-dimensional landscape that maps a molecule's geometry to
its potential energy, governing all chemical transformations.
• Low Energy = Stable: Points in the valleys of the
landscape are stable arrangements of the atoms.
• High Energy = Unstable: Points on the hills or
peaks are unstable.
• Metastable state: a condition where a
system is stable but is not in its lowest
possible energy state,
e.g., diamond vs. graphite.
PES for water molecule

slides.title: Features of the PES: Minima & Transition States
text: Features of the PES: Minima & Transition States
• Minima (Valleys): stable chemical species, e.g., the reactants and the
products of a reaction.
• Transition States (Saddle Points): highest energy point on the lowest
energy path connecting two minima (a reactant and a product)

slides.title: Thermodynamics: Will a Reaction Happen?
text: Thermodynamics: Will a Reaction Happen?
• Spontaneity: Gibbs free energy difference (ΔG=ΔH−TΔS) decides if the
reaction happens or not.
• Kinetics: activation energy
governs the reaction rate.
